client: I've been really stressed about work lately. After my team missed that big deadline last week, I can't stop worrying that I'm failing as a project manager. I know therapy is supposed to help with stress, but I'm not sure how talking about it will change the actual workload I'm dealing with.
therapist: It sounds like missing that deadline has left you feeling overwhelmed and questioning your abilities, which is completely understandable given the situation. While therapy might not reduce your workload directly, it can help us explore how you're interpreting these events and develop strategies to manage stress more effectively. What thoughts tend to come up when you start worrying about failing as a project manager?

client:
I keep thinking "I'm not cut out for this role" and "everyone will realize I'm incompetent." It's like my mind jumps to worst-case scenarios even though I've handled tough projects before. The more I try to push these thoughts away, the louder they get. 

I'm skeptical about strategies though - when I'm in panic mode, all the breathing exercises and positive thinking just feel like putting a bandaid on a broken leg. The real problem is that I actually might fail, you know?
therapist:
I hear how real and persistent these self-doubts feel for you, especially when they're shouting over your past successes. It makes sense that simple coping strategies feel inadequate when you're facing what feels like a genuine threat to your competence. 

Rather than trying to push these thoughts away or force positivity, what if we explored what these worst-case scenarios might be trying to tell us about what matters most to you in your work?

client:
I guess my worst-case scenario is that I'll completely fail at my job and everyone will realize I'm not as capable as they thought. But I don't know what that's supposed to tell me - I already know doing good work matters to me. That's why the anxiety is so intense. 

When you suggest exploring what these thoughts mean, it just makes me more anxious because it feels like there's some hidden truth I'm missing. I'm not sure this approach will help.
therapist:
I can see how this exploration might feel like it's adding another layer of pressure rather than helping, and I appreciate you sharing that with me. Your anxiety makes complete sense - when something matters deeply to us, our minds naturally try to protect us by sounding alarms about potential threats. 

Rather than searching for hidden meanings, would it feel more helpful if we looked at how these anxious thoughts might actually be affecting your performance at work?

client:
I get what you're saying about the anxiety affecting my work, but I don't know if focusing on that will help. When I'm in meetings, my mind just goes blank and I panic about saying something stupid. It's like my brain shuts down completely, and then I feel even worse afterward because I didn't contribute. 

I guess I'm worried that analyzing this will just make me more self-conscious at work. Isn't that going to make the problem worse?
therapist:
It sounds like you're caught in a cycle where the fear of underperforming actually creates the very situation you're worried about, which then reinforces those initial fears. That must feel incredibly frustrating when you're already putting so much pressure on yourself to do well.  

Instead of analyzing in the moment, would you be open to exploring some small experiments we could try to gently test whether these feared outcomes actually happen when you contribute differently?

client:
I get what you're saying about the cycle, but I don't know if "small experiments" would help. Every time I try to contribute less at work, I immediately panic that people will notice and think I'm slacking off. It's not just about outcomes - the anxiety itself is unbearable in the moment. 

What if I try to hold back and then someone actually does call me out on it? That would confirm all my worst fears.
therapist:
I hear how deeply unsettling this anxiety feels in the moment, and how even the idea of experimenting with small changes brings up fears of being "caught" underperforming. That immediate physical panic response makes it feel impossible to try anything different, even when logically you know the current approach isn't working.  

Rather than focusing on changing your work behaviors right away, would it feel safer to first explore what happens if we simply observe these anxious moments with curiosity when they arise?

client:
I get what you're saying about observing the anxiety, but I don't know if that'll help. When the panic hits, it's like my brain short-circuits - I can't just step back and watch it happen. It feels too overwhelming in the moment to be "curious" about it. 

Part of me worries that if I don't immediately fight the anxiety, it'll just take over completely. Like observing it would be giving it permission to stay.
therapist:
It makes complete sense that observing the anxiety feels impossible when it's at its peak - that overwhelming intensity is exactly what makes it so hard to work with in the moment. Your mind is understandably trying to protect you by fighting it, even though that struggle often feeds the cycle.  

What if we practiced observing the *aftermath* of these anxious episodes first, when the intensity has subsided a bit, to build that skill when you're not in crisis mode?

client: I see what you're saying about practicing after the anxiety passes, but I'm not sure it'll help in the moment when I really need it. The worst part is when I'm in the middle of a panic attack and feel completely out of control - looking back later doesn't seem as useful. Plus, when I'm not anxious, I just want to forget about those feelings, not revisit them.
therapist:
I hear how the immediate overwhelm feels like the real challenge, and how revisiting those feelings afterward might bring up resistance when you'd rather move on. That makes perfect sense - our natural instinct is to avoid what feels painful.  

Would you be willing to explore what happens if we approach these reflections not as reliving the anxiety, but as gathering information about what helps you regain that sense of control when it matters most?

client:
I get what you're saying about gathering information instead of reliving the anxiety, but honestly even that sounds exhausting. When I'm already drained from an anxious episode, the last thing I want to do is pick it apart. It feels like poking at a bruise. 

I do want to feel more in control though. Maybe if we could find a way to do this that doesn't make me feel worse afterward? I'm just worried it'll send me spiraling again.
therapist:
It sounds like you're looking for approaches that feel supportive rather than retraumatizing, and that honor your need for recovery after these draining episodes. That self-awareness about what you can handle is actually a really important protective skill.  

What if we started by simply noticing one small physical sensation that helps you feel grounded when the anxiety begins to ease, without diving into analysis at all?

client:
I like the idea of focusing on small physical sensations, but I'm not sure I'll be able to notice anything when I'm in that panicked state. My mind just races so fast during those moments that even trying to focus on my body feels impossible. 

Also, I worry that if I try this and fail, it'll just make me feel worse about myself for not being able to do something that seems so simple. That happens to me a lot with coping strategies - they work for other people but not for me.
therapist:
It makes complete sense that trying to focus inward during panic feels impossible when your mind is racing, and that past experiences with strategies failing have left you understandably hesitant. That self-protective skepticism is actually valuable information about what hasn't worked for you before.  

Rather than expecting yourself to notice sensations during full-blown panic, what if we practiced this at a time when you're only mildly anxious, where the stakes feel lower and success might feel more possible?

client: I guess that makes sense in theory, but even when I'm just mildly anxious, my mind still jumps to worst-case scenarios. It's like my brain won't let me focus on anything except what could go wrong. I've tried breathing exercises before when I was only a little anxious, and it just made me more aware of how fast my heart was beating.
therapist:
It sounds like even mild anxiety quickly pulls your attention toward catastrophic thinking, and that focusing on your body sometimes amplifies rather than soothes the discomfort. That's actually really common when we try to force relaxation before we've built enough trust in the process.  

What if instead of trying to change or control these sensations, we simply practiced noticing when your attention gets pulled toward worry, without judging whether that's good or bad?
